blocks.response_text: Hornsea One was under construction offshore: two modules were fully installed and the third partially, giving a declared export capability of 800 MW [reported]. Before the event Hornsea 1B was operating at 400 MW [reported], its maximum, and the site was generating 799 MW [reported].

The 400 kV voltage was steady at about 400 kV [reported] until 16:52:33:490 [reported]. Our reactive compensation control first injected reactive power to support the voltage, then a significant oscillation followed: we absorbed more than 300 MVAr [reported], depressing the voltage to about 394 kV [reported], and active power fell from 799 MW [reported] to 400 MW [reported] before returning to 799 MW. At 16:52:33:700 [reported] reactive power passed about 0 MVAr and the site then absorbed about 560 MVAr [reported].

In the 34 kV [reported] collection system the voltage fell rapidly to 20 kV [reported]. Trying to hold full active power at that voltage overloaded each turbine on Hornsea 1B and 1C, and their overcurrent protection de-loaded them, as the industry standard protection does to avoid permanent damage. The de-load ran from 16:52:33:728 to 16:52:33:835 [reported], 107 ms [reported]; Hornsea 1A stayed in operation at 62 MW [reported].

Our report concludes that the de-load was caused by an unexpected wind farm control system response, due to an insufficiently damped electrical resonance in the sub-synchronous frequency range, which was triggered by the initial event.
At first we understood the Dynamic Reactive Compensator to be responsible for the rapid de-load. We have since concluded that the DRC worked as designed and was not the cause.

Our internal network had one SGT and one OTSUA circuit on outage. That configuration was a contributory factor because it created a weak internal network environment; we have since reviewed and reconfigured it. Our systems identified a weak grid before detecting the voltage disturbance.

After the event we identified electrical oscillations before it that caused no de-loading: 10 minutes [reported] before, the reactive power response to a 2% [reported] voltage step change was a damped oscillatory response from the overall voltage control systems.

A control system software update performed on 10 August 2019 [reported], previously agreed with the manufacturer, mitigates the observed behaviour. Ofgem records, from information we gave it, that the update had been planned for 13 August [reported].

Each stage had been modelled and physically tested in line with grid code requirements, and the potential for oscillations had been considered. Ofgem reports, from information we provided, that modelling with our equipment manufacturer before 9 August suggested voltage control performance issues at the full planned 1,200 MW [reported], that these were not discussed with the ESO, and that prior simulations had not foreseen such issues at 799 MW [reported].

We do not know the exact time of the lightning strike. Our report times the short circuit at 16:52:33:490 [reported] and the de-load at 16:52:33:728 to 16:52:33:835 [reported]; one passage writes the de-load as 15.52.33.728 to 15.52.33.835 [reported].

role: Operations engineer, Hornsea One offshore wind farm
